summary: Selection sort splits the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted rest, and on each step finds the minimum of the rest and swaps it into the next slot of the prefix. It always performs exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons, but it makes at most n-1 swaps, which is the fewest writes of any common comparison sort. That makes it a sensible choice only when writes are very expensive and n is small, and it is a classic interview topic for explaining stability, adaptivity and the difference between comparisons and data movement.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Selection sort is built on a simple idea: to sort an array, repeatedly **select** the smallest element you have not placed yet and put it where it belongs. Position 0 must hold the global minimum, so scan the whole array, find it, and swap it into slot 0. Position 1 must hold the minimum of what remains, so scan from index 1, find it, and swap it into slot 1. After `n-1` rounds the array is sorted, because the last element is automatically the largest. The algorithm does no clever work to avoid comparisons: it scans the entire unsorted region every single time, whether or not the data was already in order. Its one real selling point is that each round performs a single swap, so the total number of element moves is linear while the number of comparisons is quadratic.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Sorted prefix**: indexes `0..i-1` hold the `i` smallest values in final order after round `i`. These elements are never touched again.
**Unsorted region**: indexes `i..n-1`. Each round scans all of it to find the minimum.
**Selection**: finding the index of the smallest element in the unsorted region with a linear scan. You track the **index** of the minimum, not just its value, so you can swap later.
**Swap once per round**: after the scan, exchange `a[i]` with `a[min]`. If `min == i` the swap can be skipped.
**Not adaptive**: the number of comparisons is the same, `n(n-1)/2`, for sorted, reversed and random input.
**Not stable (usual form)**: the long-distance swap can jump an element over equal elements and reorder them. Example: `[4a, 4b, 1]` becomes `[1, 4b, 4a]`.
**In place**: only the loop indexes and a temporary are needed, so extra space is O(1).
**Loop invariant**: at the start of round `i`, `a[0..i-1]` is sorted and every element in it is less than or equal to every element in `a[i..n-1]`.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: Sort `[64, 25, 12, 22, 11]`. Round 0: scan all five values, the minimum is 11 at index 4. Swap it with index 0 to get `[11, 25, 12, 22, 64]`. Round 1: scan indexes 1 to 4, the minimum is 12 at index 2. Swap with index 1 to get `[11, 12, 25, 22, 64]`. Round 2: scan indexes 2 to 4, the minimum is 22 at index 3. Swap with index 2 to get `[11, 12, 22, 25, 64]`. Round 3: scan indexes 3 to 4, the minimum is 25 already at index 3, so no swap is needed. The loop ends after `n-1 = 4` rounds and the last element 64 is already in place. Total: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons and 3 real swaps. You can see that the comparison count did not depend on how ordered the data was, only on `n`.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Standard (swap) version**: as shown. At most `n-1` swaps, not stable.

**Stable version**: instead of swapping, take the minimum out and shift the elements between `i` and `min` one slot right, then insert the minimum at `i`. Stability is restored, but the shifts add up to O(n^2) writes, losing the main advantage.

**Bidirectional (double) selection sort**: each scan finds both the minimum and the maximum, placing them at both ends. It halves the number of rounds and does about the same comparisons if you use the paired-comparison trick, but the code needs care when the max is at position `i`.
**Maximum-first selection sort**: select the largest and put it at the end, shrinking the range from the right. Equivalent in cost; handy for linked lists or when the tail is easier to extend.
**Heap sort**: selection sort where the selection step uses a binary heap to find the minimum in O(log n) instead of O(n), giving O(n log n). It is the natural upgrade of the same idea.

**Selection sort on a linked list**: find the minimum node, unlink it and append to the result list. No swaps of values are needed, and the sort becomes stable if you take the first minimum and append in order.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Comparisons**: exactly `n(n-1)/2` in every case. For `n = 1000` that is 499,500; for `n = 10,000` it is about 50 million.
**Swaps**: at most `n-1`, so Theta(n) data movement. With the `min != i` guard the count is the number of rounds where the minimum was not already in place.
**Time**: Theta(n^2) best, average and worst. There is no input that makes it faster.
**Space**: O(1) auxiliary.
**Stability**: not stable in the swap form. **Adaptivity**: none.

**Writes versus insertion sort**: insertion sort averages about `n^2/4` single-element shifts, and selection sort at most `n-1` swaps, i.e. about `3(n-1)` writes. This is why selection sort is preferred when a write costs much more than a read.
**Cache behaviour**: the inner scan is a sequential read, which the hardware prefetcher handles well, so it is quick for tiny arrays but loses badly to O(n log n) sorts beyond a few dozen elements.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Tracking the value instead of the index**: if you store `min_val = a[j]` you cannot swap afterwards. Keep `min` as an index.
**Using `<=` in the scan**: `a[j] <= a[min]` picks the last equal minimum rather than the first, which changes which duplicate moves and can make the reordering of equal keys worse.
**Assuming it is stable**: sorting records by key with the swap version can scramble equal-key records. If you need a multi-key sort by running two passes, use a stable sort.

**Off-by-one on the outer loop**: running to `i < n` is harmless but wasteful (one extra empty scan); starting the inner loop at `j = i` instead of `i + 1` makes one useless self-comparison per round.
**Overflow in comparison by subtraction**: writing `a[j] - a[min] < 0` can overflow for large ints. Compare directly.
**Thinking fewer swaps means faster**: for in-memory integers the swap is cheap and the comparisons dominate, so selection sort is usually slower than insertion sort on the same data.
**Using it on large data**: the O(n^2) comparisons make it unsuitable beyond a few thousand elements no matter how cheap the swaps are.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
sections.body: Selection sort is rare in production code, but its low write count has real niches. On devices with limited write endurance (EEPROM or flash memory cells that wear out), sorting small tables in place with at most `n-1` writes is attractive. In tiny embedded firmware where code size matters more than speed, a ten-line selection sort for an array of under about 20 entries is common. It is the conceptual base for heap sort and tournament sort, and for priority-queue-based scheduling (pick the minimum, remove it, repeat). Some library sorts use it indirectly: partial selection (finding the k smallest) is what `std::nth_element` and `std::partial_sort` generalise, and when `k` is tiny repeated selection is competitive. It also appears in education, because the loop invariant and the swap count make a clean case study.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Time and space?** Theta(n^2) comparisons always, O(1) space.
**How many swaps?** At most `n-1`, which is minimal among simple comparison sorts.
**Is it stable?** Not in the standard form; show `[4a, 4b, 1]` as a counterexample. A shifting version is stable.
**Is it adaptive?** No. Sorted input still costs `n(n-1)/2` comparisons.
**When would you choose it?** When writes are far more expensive than reads and `n` is small.
**Relation to heap sort?** Heap sort is selection sort with a heap to make the selection O(log n).
**Selection versus bubble?** Same comparisons order, but selection does O(n) swaps against O(n^2) for bubble.
**Can you find the k-th smallest with it?** Yes, run `k` rounds, O(nk); quickselect does it in O(n) average.

subtopics.title: Loop invariant and correctness
subtopics.summary: The argument that every round leaves a valid sorted prefix.

sections.body: Claim: at the start of round `i`, the prefix `a[0..i-1]` holds the `i` smallest elements of the original array in sorted order. Initially the prefix is empty, so the claim holds. In round `i` the inner scan finds the index of the smallest element in `a[i..n-1]`. Because the prefix elements are all no larger than anything in the suffix, placing that minimum at index `i` extends the sorted prefix by one element and keeps the property. The swap only exchanges two elements within the suffix region, so the multiset of values is unchanged. After round `n-2` the prefix has `n-1` elements, and the single leftover is no smaller than any of them, so the array is sorted.

subtopics.title: Why it is not stable
subtopics.summary: A concrete example of equal keys being reordered.

sections.body: Start with `[4a, 4b, 1]` where `4a` and `4b` are records with equal keys. Round 0 finds the minimum 1 at index 2 and swaps it with index 0, giving `[1, 4b, 4a]`. The equal keys have now exchanged their relative order, and nothing in later rounds can restore it. The cause is the swap, which carries the old `a[i]` to a faraway slot behind other equal elements. This matters whenever you sort records by one key after sorting by another (for example by city then by name) because that technique depends on stability.

subtopics.title: Making it stable
subtopics.summary: Shift instead of swap, at a cost in writes.

sections.body: To keep equal elements in order, remove the minimum and shift the block `a[i..min-1]` one position to the right, then drop the minimum into slot `i`. Always choose the first occurrence of the minimum, using strict `<` in the scan. This is stable, but the shift writes up to `n-i` elements per round, so total writes grow to O(n^2), the same as insertion sort. In practice, if you need stability you should just use insertion sort or a stable O(n log n) sort. The only context where this is worth knowing is linked lists, where removing a node and re-inserting it costs O(1) and stability is free.

Round `i` scans `n-1-i` pairs, so total comparisons are the sum of `n-1` down to 1, which is `n(n-1)/2`. For 5 elements that is 10, for 100 it is 4,950, for 10,000 it is 49,995,000. Swaps depend on the input: a sorted array needs 0 (with the guard), while a reversed array needs `floor(n/2)` real swaps for the first half of rounds, since after the early swaps the middle part falls into place. The worst case for swaps is `n-1`, but it is a theoretical bound that few inputs reach. This is the entire reason to prefer the algorithm when a write is far costlier than a read, and the reason to avoid it when comparisons are costly (for instance comparing long strings).

subtopics.title: Bidirectional selection sort
subtopics.summary: Find the min and max in the same scan.

sections.body: A double-ended version scans the unsorted window once and tracks both the minimum and the maximum index. It then swaps the minimum to the left end and the maximum to the right end and shrinks the window from both sides, so it needs only about `n/2` rounds. The comparisons per scan are still about `2 * window` unless you compare elements in pairs first, in which case it drops to about `1.5 * window`. The tricky case: if the maximum happens to sit at the left end `lo`, then after swapping the minimum into `lo` the maximum has moved to the old position of the minimum, so you must update the max index before the second swap. Missing this is the classic bug.

subtopics.title: Selection sort on linked lists
subtopics.summary: Relink nodes instead of swapping values.

sections.body: On a singly linked list you can find the node with the smallest key, unlink it from the source list in O(1) given its predecessor, and append it to the tail of a result list. Repeating this until the source is empty gives a sorted list in O(n^2) time with O(1) extra space and no value copying, which matters when nodes are large. Always pick the first minimum and append to the tail to keep the sort stable. For production code a merge sort on the list is better, at O(n log n), but the selection approach is easy to write correctly in an interview.

subtopics.title: From selection sort to heap sort

sections.body: The expensive part of selection sort is the O(n) scan that finds the next minimum. If you build a binary heap first (O(n)), the minimum is always at the root, and removing it costs O(log n) because you swap the last element to the root and sift it down. Doing that `n` times gives O(n log n) total. In heap sort the same array holds both the heap and the growing sorted region, which keeps the O(1) extra space. A max-heap puts the largest elements at the end of the array, mirroring the max-first selection sort. Heap sort is not stable, and has worse cache behaviour than quick sort, but its guaranteed O(n log n) bound is why it is used inside introsort as a fallback.

Use selection sort when all of these hold: the array is tiny (about 20 or fewer elements), each write is expensive or limited (flash, EEPROM, remote memory), stability does not matter, and code size is tight. Use insertion sort if the data may be nearly sorted or you need stability. Use the standard library sort (`qsort`, `std::sort`) for everything else. For finding only the smallest `k` items, use a heap or `nth_element`. In an interview, mention that selection sort minimises swaps but not comparisons, and that both matter depending on the cost model.

subtopics.title: Selection sort versus cycle sort and the write count
subtopics.summary: Where selection sort sits among low-write algorithms.

sections.body: Selection sort needs at most `n-1` swaps, which is far fewer memory writes than bubble or insertion sort, and only **cycle sort** writes less: cycle sort writes each element at most once, directly into its final position, and so performs the theoretical minimum number of writes for an in-place sort. If someone asks which simple sort to pick when writes are costly, the answer is cycle sort first and selection sort second. Selection sort stays popular because it is far simpler. The five quick answers worth memorising: it is not stable (equal elements can change relative order), time is O(n^2) in the best, average and worst cases, extra space is O(1) (in place), it suits small data sets, teaching, and cases where memory use or writes must be minimal, and it differs from bubble sort by selecting the minimum and placing it with one swap per round, while bubble sort swaps adjacent pairs repeatedly. The nested loops explain the O(n^2): the outer loop runs `n-1` times and the inner scan is up to `n` long.

takeaways: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into the next position of the sorted prefix.
It always makes exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons, so best, average and worst time are all Theta(n^2).
It makes at most n-1 swaps, the fewest among the simple comparison sorts, which suits expensive writes.
The usual swap-based version is not stable: [4a, 4b, 1] becomes [1, 4b, 4a].
Space is O(1), and the algorithm is not adaptive to presorted input.
Track the index of the minimum, not its value, so you can swap after the scan.
Heap sort is selection sort with a heap making each selection O(log n).
